metadata.scope: e_wendish_empire (all baronies across k_esthonia and k_lithuania)

schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if not extracted from retrieved summary and flagged for manual check).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true if the barony title name is historically authentic for the 867 AD start date; false if anachronistic or unattested <= 867 (candidate for Step 2 resolution).
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person/dynasty/settler after 867 AD.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or other natural topographic feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with source language and English translation.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name STRICTLY ATTESTED <= 867 AD exists for the settlement (or its immediate predecessor site / base name without a post-867 modifier). Every exists=true entry carries first_mention_year <= 867.

b_narva.first_mention_attestation: 1172 CE in the First Novgorod Chronicle (Nerevsky/Narovsky konets); Narvia village attested in 1241 CE in the Danish Census Book.
b_narva.etymology_analysis: Named after the Narva River (attested 1221 CE). The hydronym is most commonly linked by Finnic linguists (e.g., Lauri Kettunen) to a Finnic/Vepsian root narva meaning 'threshold' or 'rapids', referring to the Narva waterfalls; alternative hypotheses propose a Germanic (*narwaz 'narrow') or Slavic origin.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Narva (ancient river crossing settlement on the Narva River) (in-game: Narwe)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Constituent capital seat disambiguated from ancient Estonian stronghold Tarvanpää.

b_wesenburg.first_mention_attestation: 1252 CE as Wesenbergh in Middle Low German records (preceded by Estonian Tarwanpe in 1226 CE in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry).
b_wesenburg.etymology_analysis: Middle Low German adaptation and partial calque of the Estonian hillfort name Tarvanpää ('aurochs's head', attested 1226 CE), combining wesen ('aurochs/bison') with bergh ('hill/fortress').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Estonian stronghold Tarvanpää ('Bull's Head', attested 1226) (in-game: Tarvanpää)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 native toponym restored over post-867 colonial foundation.

b_poltsamaa.first_mention_attestation: 1272 CE upon the founding of the Livonian Order castle Oberpahlen/Overpalen; the surrounding Mõhu (Moche) district is attested in 1234 CE.
b_poltsamaa.etymology_analysis: Estonian Põltsamaa derives from põld ('field', reconstructed *põldus / *põltoisa 'rich in fields') + maa ('land'), meaning 'land of fields'. Known in German as Oberpahlen ('upper Pahlen/pale') and in Russian chronicles as Polchev.

b_kuressare.first_mention_attestation: 1381 CE in Latin texts as arx aquilae (German Arensburg) for the episcopal castle; Estonian Kurresare Linna attested by 1710 CE.

morphemes.translation: crane (genitive of kurg) or large bird

b_kuressare.etymology_analysis: Estonian Kuressaare combines kure ('crane', genitive of kurg) and saar ('island'), either from an older name of Saaremaa or as a folk reinterpretation of the eagle (German Arensburg, Latin arx aquilae) on the coat of arms of the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Sâremâ — Historical Option A seat of c_osel

b_maasilinna.first_mention_attestation: 1345 CE when the Livonian Order castle (German Soneburg) was established by Landmeister Burchard von Dreileben.
b_maasilinna.etymology_analysis: Estonian Maasilinn(a) means 'fortress of Maasi' (from the nearby village of Maasi + linn 'fortress'). In German it was called Soneburg ('atonement/punishment castle') because it was built as a punitive stronghold after the St. George's Night Uprising (1343–1345 CE).

b_muhu.first_mention_attestation: 1227 CE as Mone in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry (and 1228 CE as Mona).

morphemes.translation: bump, mound, or boggy land (disputed; cf. Swedish Moon)

b_muhu.etymology_analysis: Island name attested in 1227 CE as Mone. Linguists have connected Estonian Muhu to muhk ('mound/elevation') or muhu ('boggy ground'), or alternatively to the historical Swedish name Moon ('white sand', borrowed into German as Mohn/Moon).

b_hiiumaa.first_mention_attestation: 1575 CE as Hioma in written records (the island was earlier attested in 1228 CE as Dageida).
b_hiiumaa.etymology_analysis: Estonian Hiiumaa combines hiis (genitive hiiu, originally 'sacred grove' or 'burial place', cf. Finnish Hiidenmaa) and maa ('land'). The older 1228 CE Latin/Germanic attestation Dageida (Swedish Dagö) reflects Old Gutnish Dagaiþ ('day isthmus').

b_reval.first_mention_attestation: 1219 CE / c. 1227 CE as Reval / Revalia following the Danish conquest of northern Estonia (derived from the adjacent county Revala/Revele).

morphemes.translation: name of the ancient Estonian coastal county (etymology uncertain)

b_reval.etymology_analysis: Reval (Latin Revalia, Old Norse Rafala) is the German and Scandinavian name for Tallinn, taken from the surrounding ancient Estonian county of Revala (Rävala) after the 1219 CE Danish conquest. The Estonian name Tallinn derives from Taani-linna ('Danish castle').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Finnic/Estonian settlement Lindanisa (attested before 1219 Danish crusade fortress) (in-game: Lindanisa)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 native toponym restored over post-867 colonial foundation.

b_harjumaa.first_mention_attestation: 1212 CE as Harien in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry (and 1219–1241 CE as Hæriæ / Harriæn in the Danish Census Book).
b_harjumaa.etymology_analysis: Ancient Estonian province name (Latin Harria, German Harrien). Most scholars connect Harju to Estonian (mäe)hari ('mountain/hill ridge', cf. Finnish harju 'ridge') + maa ('land').

b_jarva.first_mention_attestation: 1212 CE as Gerwiam / Gerwa in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry (and 1214 CE as Yereva in the First Novgorod Chronicle).

morphemes.translation: lake, wetland (loaned from Baltic *jaura 'marsh, boggy land')

b_jarva.etymology_analysis: Ancient Estonian province name (Latin Jervia/Gerwia, German Jerwen). Derived from Estonian järv ('lake'), which Enn Tarvel traces to a Baltic loanword *jaura ('marshy/wetland area'), reflecting the region's historic bogs.

b_hapsal.first_mention_attestation: 1279 CE as Hapsal in the town charter granted by the Bishop of Ösel-Wiek.
b_hapsal.etymology_analysis: German and Swedish Hapsal is an adaptation of Estonian Haapsalu, compounded from haab ('aspen') and salu (archaically '(forested) island', modern 'grove'), meaning 'aspen grove/island'.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Rîdale — Historical Option A seat of c_wiek

b_leal.first_mention_attestation: 1211 CE as Leale in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry (also seat of the Diocese of Leal).

morphemes.translation: uncertain (possibly from liha or lehu 'mud', or an ancient hillfort name)

b_leal.etymology_analysis: Leal (1211 CE Leale) is the Germanized form of Estonian Lihula, an ancient Estonian hillfort and parish center whose etymology remains uncertain.

b_tartu.first_mention_attestation: 1224 CE as Tarbatum / Darbete in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry (the site was earlier attested in 1030 CE as Yuryev in the Primary Chronicle).
b_tartu.etymology_analysis: Estonian Tartu (and German Dorpat) evolved from ancient Estonian *Tarvatu (attested in Latin as Tarbatum/Darbete), meaning 'place abounding in aurochs' (tarvas + -tu). In 1030 CE, Yaroslav the Wise briefly named the fort Yuryev after his baptismal name.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Tarbâte — Historical Option A seat of c_dorpat

b_vastseliina.first_mention_attestation: 1342 CE when the border fortress was founded (initially called Frauenburg, later Neuhausen / Vastseliina).
b_vastseliina.etymology_analysis: South Estonian Vastseliina (Võro Vahtsõliina) literally means 'new castle', corresponding to German Neuhausen and Latin Novum castrum, distinguishing the 1342 CE fortress from older Kirumpää Castle.

b_valga.first_mention_attestation: 1286 CE as Walko in the credit register of the city of Riga.
b_valga.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1286 CE as Walko (German Walk, Latvian Valka, Estonian Valga). The etymology is uncertain; proposals include a Finnic root valk- ('white/light'), Latvian valks ('stream'), or Russian volok ('boat portage').

b_parnu.first_mention_attestation: 1251 CE as Perona (Old Pärnu, founded by the Bishop of Ösel-Wiek; river attested as Perona in 1260 CE; 1154 CE Barnū in al-Idrisi is uncertain).

morphemes.translation: river name (cf. Veps pern 'steep riverbank' or Estonian pärn 'linden')

b_parnu.etymology_analysis: Derived from the river name Perona (1260 CE, German Pernau). While folk etymology links it to Estonian pärn ('linden tree'), linguists also propose a pre-Finnic substrate hydronym, a Baltic origin, or Vepsian pern ('steep riverbank').

b_viljandi.first_mention_attestation: 1211 CE in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry (Viliende); town charter recorded in 1283 CE.
b_viljandi.etymology_analysis: Estonian Viljandi (early 13th-century Viliende, German Fellin) is derived from Estonian vili ('grain, crop, fruit') with the suffix -ndi. An alleged 1154 CE mention (FLMWS) in al-Idrisi is widely rejected by Estonian scholars.

b_alistegunde.first_mention_attestation: 1211 CE as Alistegunde in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry (XV.7).
b_alistegunde.etymology_analysis: Ancient Estonian parish (muinaskihelkond) in southern Sakala, recorded in 1211 CE as Alistegunde (modern Estonian Alistekund, later Halliste). Combines *aline ('lower') with the Finnic territorial suffix -kund ('district/parish').

b_riga.first_mention_attestation: 1198–1201 CE in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry (Bishop Berthold's campaign in 1198 CE and Bishop Albert's founding of Riga in 1201 CE).

morphemes.translation: threshing barn, granary/warehouse (or Rīdzene stream / ringa 'loop')

b_riga.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1201 CE at an earlier Livonian trading port (portus antiquus). The name Riga most reliably derives from Livonian/Latvian rīja ('granary/warehouse' along the Daugava), or alternatively from the Rīdzene (Riege) tributary or Livonian ringa ('loop').

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Vidzeme is a late medieval division ('Middle Land'). Ancient pre-867 reach is the river Gauja.

b_lemisele.first_mention_attestation: 1223 CE in historical tradition for Bishop Albert's castle at Lemsal/Lemisele (town rights granted in 1385 CE).
b_lemisele.etymology_analysis: Livonian settlement name Lemisele (also Lembsele, German Lemsal/Lemsahl, modern Latvian Limbaži), meaning 'wide isle in a forest swamp' in Livonian.

b_salacgriva.first_mention_attestation: 1391 CE as Saltze in the Lübeck Chronicle (referring to the Archbishop of Riga's castle at the earlier Livonian settlement of Saletsa).
b_salacgriva.etymology_analysis: Latvian Salacgrīva literally means 'mouth of the Salaca River' (German Salismünde), combining the river name Salaca (from Livonian Saletsa) with Latvian grīva ('river mouth').

b_grobin.first_mention_attestation: 1253 CE Curonian partition treaty between the Bishop of Courland and the Livonian Order (Grobin); Teutonic castle built in the 13th century CE.
b_grobin.etymology_analysis: Germanized as Grobin from a Curonian/Baltic root, often linked to Baltic *grab-/*skrobl- ('hornbeam') or *grāvis ('ditch, moat'), adapted into Latvian as Grobiņa.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Resolved via verified historical center Sêburch documented in tarraconian_titles_1059.md.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Rimbert, Vita Ansgari (c. 875 CE, describing events of c. 854 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Rimbert's Vita Ansgari records that King Olof of Sweden captured and burned the Curonian coastal stronghold of Seeburg (usually identified with Grobiņa) in c. 854 CE.

b_bandava.first_mention_attestation: 1231 CE treaty between papal vice-legate Baldwin of Alna and the Curonians (Latin: Bandowe); partitioned in 1253 CE.

morphemes.translation: herd, cattle, or allotted plot of land (cf. Latvian banda)

b_bandava.etymology_analysis: Curonian regional name (Latinized as Bandowe) derived from Baltic *banda ('herd, cattle' or 'allotted land') with the Baltic toponymic suffix -ava.

older_name_by_867.notes: Rimbert's Vita Ansgari (c. 875 CE) mentions five Curonian civitates without naming Bandava; the name Bandowe is first attested in 1231 CE.

b_duvzare.first_mention_attestation: 1252–1253 CE treaties between the Livonian Order and the Bishopric of Courland (attested as Dovsare, Dovzare, Duizare).
b_duvzare.etymology_analysis: Curonian land name (Dovsare, Duizare), analyzed by Kazimieras Būga as Curonian *duvi + *ezars ('two lakes' or 'branched lake', referring to Lake Pape) or West Baltic *donis + *azaran ('sacred/gift lake').

b_ceklis.first_mention_attestation: 1252 CE treaty between the Livonian Master and the Bishop of Courland regarding Memel/Klaipėda Castle (Latin: Ceclis).

morphemes.translation: clearing, scrubland, or corner/region (uncertain Baltic root)

b_ceklis.etymology_analysis: Curonian regional name (Latin: Ceclis; Lithuanian: Ceklis / Keklys) of Baltic origin, first recorded in 1252–1253 CE partition acts of southern Courland.

b_selpils.first_mention_attestation: 1208 CE in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia, recording the capture of the Selonian stronghold (castrum Selonum / Sēlpils).
b_selpils.etymology_analysis: Compound of the ethnonym Sēļi (Selonians) and Latvian pils ('castle, hillfort'), meaning 'castle of the Selonians' (German: Selburg).

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Resolved via verified historical center Sêlônjen documented in tarraconian_titles_1059.md.

b_oknist.first_mention_attestation: 1298 CE historical sources mentioning Aknīste (German: Oknist; Lithuanian: Aknysta).
b_oknist.etymology_analysis: Baltic toponym (Latvian Aknīste, Lithuanian Aknysta, German Oknist) derived from a local Baltic hydronym.

b_piltene.first_mention_attestation: 1295 CE historical records mentioning Piltene (German: Pilten), seat of the Bishopric of Courland (a 1220 CE Danish castle tradition is unverified).
b_piltene.etymology_analysis: Toponym (Latvian Piltene, Livonian Piltõn, German Pilten) associated with Baltic *pil- ('fort, castle, earthwork') or Finnic/Livonian coastal trading-post terminology.

b_dundaga.first_mention_attestation: 1245 CE charter of Bishop Nicholas of Riga granting land in Donedange (Dundaga) to the Riga Cathedral chapter.

morphemes.translation: reed, marshy corner, or Finnic/Baltic root

b_dundaga.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1245 CE as Donedange (Livonian: Dūoņig; German: Dondangen), reflecting Curonian-Livonian contact in northern Courland.

b_kandava.first_mention_attestation: 1230 CE peace treaty between the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, Riga, and Curonians of the Abava valley (Latin: villa Candowe).

morphemes.translation: stump, edge, or bend (cf. Baltic *kand- / Livonian kāndav)

b_kandava.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1230 CE as villa Candowe (German: Kandau, Livonian: Kāndav), a Curonian hillfort center in Vanema formed with the Baltic suffix -ava.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Curonian hillfort Candeve (attested 1230 in treaty of Balduin von Alna) (in-game: Kandava)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic Curonian hillfort.

b_uxkull.first_mention_attestation: 1184–1185 CE in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia (Ykescola / Ykescole), when Saint Meinhard arrived to missionize the Livonians.
b_uxkull.eponym_details: According to linguist Urmas Sutrop, named after a 12th-century CE Livonian local ruler named Ike (Ike's son's ford/islet, Ykescola).
b_uxkull.etymology_analysis: Germanized as Üxküll (modern Latvian Ikšķile) from Livonian Ykescola/Ykescole. Urmas Sutrop derives it from a Livonian term meaning the Daugava ford or islet belonging to the son of local ruler Ike (rejecting the older folk etymology ikš-ķile 'one village').

b_dobele.first_mention_attestation: 1254 CE German document mentioning the Semigallian wooden fortress as Dubelene or Dubelone.
b_dobele.etymology_analysis: Reconstructed as Semigallian *Dobelene (German: Doblen), derived from Baltic duobe ('pit, hollow') and duobele ('dip, dimple'), meaning a settlement in a hollow or depression.

b_mitau.first_mention_attestation: 1265 CE construction of the Livonian Order castle of Mitau (Mītava) on an island in the Lielupe River.
b_mitau.etymology_analysis: German name Mitau (used until 1917 CE) is explained either from Latvian mīt ('to trade/exchange', i.e. trading place) or German Mitte in der Aue ('middle of the Aa/Lielupe river-meadow'); the modern Latvian name Jelgava derives from Livonian jālgab ('town on the river').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Semigallian Lielupe river crossing (replacing 1265 Livonian castle Mitau) (in-game: Mitau)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1265 Livonian castle Mitau fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to native Jelgava.

b_bauska.first_mention_attestation: 1443 CE first mention of the construction of Bauska Castle (German: Bauske) by the Livonian Order.

morphemes.translation: poor meadow or swelling/hillock (or German Bausch)

b_bauska.etymology_analysis: First attested with the 1443 CE Livonian Order castle (German: Bauske). Linguist Jānis Endzelīns linked Latvian bauska to an archaic word for a poor/marshy meadow, while other hypotheses connect it to German Bausch ('bend, hillock').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Semigallian Mūša/Mēmele river confluence (replacing 1443 Livonian castle Bauska) (in-game: Bauska)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1443 Livonian castle Bauska fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to native Semigallian stem.

b_neuenburg.first_mention_attestation: 1411 CE list of Livonian Order castles (attested as Nuwenburg, later Nienborch, Neuenburg; Latvian: Jaunpils).
b_neuenburg.etymology_analysis: Middle Low German Nuwenburg / High German Neuenburg ('new castle'), built by the Livonian Order in the late 14th century CE and calqued into Latvian as Jaunpils ('new castle').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Curonian hillfort Jaunpils (replacing 14th-century Livonian castle Neuenburg) (in-game: Neuenburg)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 14th-century Livonian castle Neuenburg fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to Curonian hillfort.

b_aluksne.first_mention_attestation: 1284 CE in the Pskov Chronicles under the names Olysta, Alyst, and Volyst (later German: Marienburg).
b_aluksne.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Latgalian word olūksna ('spring in a forest'), attested in 1284 CE in East Slavic as Olysta/Alyst; later renamed Marienburg by the Livonian Order in 1342 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Alûksne — Historical Option A seat of c_aluksne

b_gulbene.first_mention_attestation: 1224 CE Tālava partition treaty between the Livonian Brothers of the Sword and the Bishop of Riga (attested as Gulbana).
b_gulbene.etymology_analysis: Latgalian/Latvian toponym (attested as Gulbana in 1224 CE) derived from gulbis ('swan'), which was later translated into German as Schwanenburg ('swan castle') when the Archbishop of Riga built a stone castle in 1340 CE.

b_jersika.first_mention_attestation: 1203 CE in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia (Latin: Gercike / Gerzika), seat of Prince Visvaldis.

morphemes.translation: fortified town/citadel (cf. Slavic *gorodec or Baltic root)

b_jersika.etymology_analysis: Medieval Latgalian principality and hillfort attested as Gerzika/Gercike in 1203 CE (Old East Slavic Герсике), variously linked to Baltic roots or a Slavic adaptation *Gorodishche/*Zargrad.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Gersika (Jersika) on the Daugava was the ancient Latgalian hillfort documented in the Livonian Chronicle. Resolved to Gêrsike.

b_jekabpils.first_mention_attestation: 1670 CE charter by Duke Jacob Kettler granting Magdeburg town rights to Jēkabmiests (German: Jakobstadt).
b_jekabpils.eponym_details: Named after Jacob Kettler (1610–1682 CE), Duke of Courland and Semigallia, who granted the town Magdeburg rights in 1670 CE.

morphemes.translation: Jacob (personal name of Duke Jacob Kettler)

b_jekabpils.etymology_analysis: Literally 'Castle/Town of Jacob' (originally German Jakobstadt / Latvian Jēkabmiests), named in 1670 CE after Duke Jacob Kettler of Courland.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Selonian Daugava crossing and hillfort Sēlpils (replacing 1670 town Jakobstadt) (in-game: Jekabpils)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1670 ducal town Jakobstadt fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to ancient Selonian Sēlpils.

b_daugavpils.first_mention_attestation: 1275 CE construction of Dinaburg (Dünaburg) Castle by Livonian Order Master Ernst von Ratzeburg (modern Latvian Daugavpils adopted in 1920 CE).
b_daugavpils.etymology_analysis: Latvian compound 'Daugava Castle' (from the Daugava River + pils 'castle'), calquing the 1275 CE German name Dünaburg / Dinaburg ('Düna/Daugava Castle').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Daugava River basin (pre-867 Baltic hydronym, replacing 1275 Livonian Dinaburg castle) (in-game: Dôugowe)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Dinaburg castle built in 1275 by Livonian Order Master Ernst von Ratzeburg; ancient Latgalian principality seat was Jersika. Resolved via Option B to the ancient Daugava River hydronym (Dôugowe).

b_rezekne.first_mention_attestation: 1285 CE first documented mention when the Livonian Order built a stone castle (German: Rositten; Latvian: Rēzekne).

morphemes.translation: cut, channel, or stream (from the Rēzekne River)

b_rezekne.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Rēzekne River valley (Latgalian: Rēzne), first documented in 1285 CE (German: Rositten, Polish: Rzeżyca).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Latgalian Rēzekne hillfort on the Rēzekne river (replacing 1285 Livonian castle Rositten) (in-game: Rezekne)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1285 Livonian castle Rositten fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to native Latgalian hillfort.

b_kokenois.first_mention_attestation: 1205 CE in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia (Kukenois / Kokenhusen), when Prince Vyachko ceded half his land to Bishop Albert of Riga.

morphemes.translation: tree, wood, or bend (or river name)

b_kokenois.etymology_analysis: Latgalian and Selonian settlement originally attested as Kukenois in 1205 CE, Germanized as Kokenhusen and modernized in Latvian as Koknese.

b_cesvaine.first_mention_attestation: 1209 CE treaty between Bishop Albert of Riga and Visvaldis of Jersika (Latin: Urbs Zcessowe).
b_cesvaine.etymology_analysis: Ancient Latgalian hillfort attested in 1209 CE as Urbs Zcessowe (German: Seßwegen, modern Latvian: Cesvaine).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Latgalian hillfort Cessowe (attested 1209) (replacing Sesswegen) (in-game: Cesvaine)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic 1209 Latgalian hillfort.

b_lennewarden.first_mention_attestation: 1201 CE in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia, recording the Baltic hillfort Lennewarden granted in fief by Bishop Albert.

morphemes.translation: guard, ford, or enclosure (cf. Latvian vārti 'gate')

b_lennewarden.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1201 CE as Lennewarden in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia, a Germanized form of the local Baltic/Livonian Daugava hillfort name (modern Latvian: Lielvārde).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Livonian Daugava hillfort Lielvārde (in-game: Lennewarden)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic ancient Livonian Daugava hillfort.

b_valmiera.first_mention_attestation: 1323 CE first mention as a town (German: Wolmar; castle/church site from 1224/1283 CE).
b_valmiera.eponym_details: Derived from the personal name Waldemar / Vladimir, attributed either to Prince Vladimir Mstislavich of Pskov (fl. 1212–1214 CE) or King Valdemar II of Denmark (1170–1241 CE).
b_valmiera.etymology_analysis: Latvian adaptation of German Wolmar / Waldemer (East Slavic Volodimirec), derived from the personal name of either Prince Vladimir Mstislavich of Pskov (early 13th century CE) or King Valdemar II of Denmark.

b_venden.first_mention_attestation: 1206 CE in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia, recording events at the settlement of the Vends (Wenden; modern Cēsis).

morphemes.translation: Vends (tribe that settled at Riekstu Hill)

b_venden.etymology_analysis: German Wenden (Livonian: Venden), named after the Vends who inhabited the hillfort at Riekstu Hill in the 11th–12th centuries CE; the Latvian name Cēsis has an independent Baltic origin.

b_rauna.first_mention_attestation: 1381 CE first documented mention of Rauna Castle (German: Ronneburg / Rownenborgh; 18th-century tradition claims 1262 CE).
b_rauna.etymology_analysis: Named after the Rauna River, around which the medieval archbishopric castle of Rownenborgh / Ronneburg was built.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Latgalian Rauna river hillfort (replacing 1262 Archbishop castle Ronneburg) (in-game: Rauna)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1262 Archbishop castle Ronneburg fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to native Rauna hillfort.

b_braslau.first_mention_attestation: 1065 CE first mention in East Slavic chronicles as a border castle of the Principality of Polotsk (Braslav).
b_braslau.eponym_details: Derived from the East Slavic personal name *Braslavъ / Bryachislav, traditionally attributed to Prince Bryachislav Izyaslavich of Polotsk (c. 997–1044 CE).
b_braslau.etymology_analysis: Derived from the East Slavic personal name *Braslavъ (associated with Bryachislav of Polotsk) with the possessive suffix -jь, yielding Braslaw/Braslav.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Bratzlâw — Historical Option A seat of c_braslau

b_utena.first_mention_attestation: 1261 CE charter of King Mindaugas of Lithuania mentioning Utena as a center of Nalšia.
b_utena.etymology_analysis: Lithuanian toponym derived from a local Baltic hydronym (the Utena / Utenėlė stream), first attested in 1261 CE.

b_upyte.etymology_analysis: Lithuanian Upytė is a diminutive of upė ('river'), meaning 'little river/stream', first mentioned in a 1254 CE Livonian chronicle.

b_birzai.first_mention_attestation: 1455 CE first written mention of Biržai
b_birzai.etymology_analysis: Lithuanian Biržai (German: Birsen) derives from beržas ('birch'), denoting a birch grove or cleared forest tract, first attested in 1455 CE.
